{{Short description|American physical chemist and academic (1920–2020)}}
'''Murray Eden''' (August 17, 1920 &ndash; August 9, 2020), was an American [[physical chemist]] and<ref name=nci>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F5m8uvV1c1wC&pg=PA30|title=Research Fellows of the National Cancer Institute|date=1959|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office, National Cancer Institute|page=30|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Kolers|first1=Paul A.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=64pqAAAAMAAJ&q=murray+eden+chemist|title=Recognizing Patterns: Studies in Living and Automatic Systems|last2=Eden|first2=Murray|date=1968|publisher=M.I.T. Press|page=137|isbn=9780262110235 |language=en}}</ref> academic. He was a professor in electrical engineering,<ref name="eecsmit"/> a lecturer, a visiting professor and adjunct professor at institutions including at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and the [[National Institutes of Health]].<ref name=nih/>

Eden was a pioneer in the field of [[biomedical engineering]] and imaging. He was director of the trans-NIH [[Biomedical Engineering]] and NIH's Physical Science Program.<ref name=nih/>

The [[National Institutes of Health]] stated that "Dr. Murray Eden elevated the NIH Biomedical Engineering and Physical Science Program."<ref name=nih/>

Eden was born in [[Brooklyn]] on August 17, 1920, to [[Russian Jewish|Russian-Jewish]] immigrants. His father was president of the Hebrew Teachers Union, and later, Executive Secretary of the Jewish Education Committee in New York City.

Due to the [[Depression of 1920–1921|depression]], as well as pre-[[World War II]] [[anti-Semitism]], the family experienced economic difficulties during his childhood years.

He graduated at 14 from [[Townsend Harris High School]] in Manhattan in 1935, attended [[City College of New York]], 1935–39, graduated in 1939. In 1940, he moved to Washington, D.C., as a chemistry major and in 1951 received his Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]].<ref name=ethw>{{Cite web|title=Oral-History:Murray Eden - Engineering and Technology History Wiki|url=https://ethw.org/Oral-History:Murray_Eden#About_Murray_Eden|date=1999-11-10|access-date=2021-01-04|website=ethw.org}}</ref><ref name=dm/>

==Career==
During [[World War II]], {{circa|1941}}, as civil service, alongside then student [[Dick Feynman]] and others, he worked in the [[Princeton University|Princeton]] facility of the [[Manhattan Project]] assisting in producing uranium-235.<ref name=nih>{{Cite web|title=Longtime Engineering Authority Eden Mourned|url=https://nihrecord.nih.gov/2020/10/02/longtime-engineering-authority-eden-mourned|date=2020-10-02|access-date=2021-01-04|website=NIH Record|language=EN}}</ref>

Between 1949 and 1953, Murray worked at  [[National Cancer Institute]].<ref name=nci/>

Between 1959 and 1979, while working in electrical engineering, he has split his ''groundbreaking body of work'' between [[MIT]],<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mRMige9H5nUC&pg=RA3-PA249|title=Current Projects on Economic and Social Implications of Science and Technology|date=1965|publisher=National Science Foundation.|page=249|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uw82AAAAIAAJ&pg=RA2-PA683|title=Hearings, Reports and Prints of the Senate Committee on Labor and Public Welfare|date=1974|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office|page=683|language=en}}</ref> [[Harvard Medical School]], the [[NIH]] and the [[World Health Organization]].<ref name="eecsmit"/> He has made independent innovations in [[computerized tomography]] while working on [[pattern recognition]], image processing, handwritten generation & analysis, between the early 1960s-1976.<ref name=ethw/>

Murray was one four editors of [[Information and Control]] from 1961 until 1966 and sole editor-in-chief of the journal from 1967 until 1981.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eden |first=Murray |date=1967-01-01 |title=Editorial |journal=Information and Control |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=i–iii |doi=10.1016/S0019-9958(67)90012-5 |issn=0019-9958|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Meyer |first=Albert R. |date=1987-01-01 |title=A change of name |journal=Information and Computation |language=en |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=iii |doi=10.1016/0890-5401(87)90047-2 |issn=0890-5401|doi-access= }}</ref>

Murray headed the [[NIH]]'s  [[Biomedical Engineering and Instrumentation Program]] (BEIP) since 1979<ref name=tucson>{{Cite web|last=Casanova|first=Stephanie|title=Murray Eden, a biomedical engineer with a love of singing, dies in Tucson at 99|url=https://tucson.com/news/local/murray-eden-a-biomedical-engineer-with-a-love-of-singing-dies-in-tucson-at-99/article_30e24a8e-7b61-56e7-9b32-bc521fb11707.html|date=2020-08-18|access-date=2021-01-04|website=Arizona Daily Star|language=en}}</ref> and retired from BEIP in 1994.<ref name=nih1994>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B9Iy2It-qMcC&pg=RA5-PP3|title=The NIH Record|date=1994-03-15|publisher=U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, National Institutes of Health|page=7|language=en}}</ref> Since Eden's retirement, under merged leadership, the BEIP program has been facing significant challenges.<ref name=ethw/>

Eden contributed to the [[World Health Organization]],<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1966|title=Statement on communications science by Professor Murray Eden|hdl=10665/143750|url=https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/143750|language=en |author1=Executive Board 37 |website=World Health Organization}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Eden|first1=Murray|last2=Green|first2=James E.|last3=Sun|first3=Anthony|date=1973|title=Feasibility of computer screening of blood films for the detection of malaria parasites*|journal=Bulletin of the World Health Organization|language=en|volume=48|issue=2|pages=211–218|issn=0042-9686|pmid=4578363|pmc=2481007|hdl=10665/263642}}</ref> and was a consultant on [[research and development]] for its director-general.<ref name=eecsmit>{{Cite web|title=Remembering Murray Eden, 1920-2020 {{!}} MIT EECS|url=https://www.eecs.mit.edu/news-events/media/remembering-murray-eden-1920-2020|date=2020-09-01|access-date=2021-01-04|website=www.eecs.mit.edu|archive-date=2021-01-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115152905/https://www.eecs.mit.edu/news-events/media/remembering-murray-eden-1920-2020|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Murray was also a lecturer, a visiting professor or adjunct professor at various institutions, including at: [[Harvard University]], [[American University]], [[Boston University Law School]], [[Johns Hopkins University]] as well as (in the 80s<ref name=dm/> at) the Swiss [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne]].<ref name=nih1994/>

Murray Eden was also consultant on the team that created the [[Universal Product Code]] barcode.<ref name=ethw/><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=je7ugzk85CYC&pg=PA15|title=Technology Applied to the Food Industry: A Preliminary Report|date=1975|publisher=National Commission on Productivity and Work Quality|page=15|language=en}}</ref> As chairman of a committee of scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, he helped ''select a symbol that would endure the inevitable rush of technology that lay ahead.''<ref>{{Cite book|last=Haberman|first=Alan L.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yeKRAAAAIAAJ&q=Murray+Eden|title=Twenty-Five Years Behind Bars: The Proceedings of the Twenty-Fifth Anniversary of the U.P.C. at the Smithsonian Institution, September 30, 1999|date=2001|publisher=Harvard University Wertheim Publications Committee|isbn=978-0-674-00657-7|pages=74,108|language=en}}</ref><ref name="dm">{{Cite web|title=Murray Eden Obituary - Tucson, AZ|url=https://www.dignitymemorial.com/en-ca/obituaries/tucson-az/murray-eden-9304895|access-date=2021-01-17|website=Dignity Memorial|language=en}}</ref>
He chose the font, and he came up with the idea to add numbers to the bottom, which is a failsafe system, in case the code reader is down.<ref name=tucson/><ref>{{Cite web|last=Roth|first=Brad|date=2020-04-17|title=Murray Eden|url=https://bradroth.medium.com/murray-eden-740c0ab08694|access-date=2021-01-14|website=Medium|language=en}}</ref>

==Views==
Eden was an activist since early on, including being involved in peace activism.<ref name=eecsmit/>
On Darwinism he regarded "evolution" as "highly implausible."<ref>{{Cite web|title=List of Intellectual Doubters of Darwinism|url=http://www.ideacenter.org/contentmgr/showdetails.php/id/1207|access-date=2021-01-04|website=www.ideacenter.org}}</ref>

==Awards==
Eden received [[NIH]]'s  [[Biomedical Engineering and Instrumentation Program]] (BEIP)  ''Directors award'' in 1993.<ref name=tucson/>

In 1983, he was awarded the [[WHO]] [[World Health Organization#Medical Society of the World Health Organization|Medical Society]] medal, for his work as consultant on research and development for its director-general.<ref name=eecsmit/>

==Personal==
In 1945 he married Sara Baker.<ref name=ethw/> Sara was a consultant and a political and community activist. She died on September 15, 1995, at the age of 73.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Sara Shriver, Community Activist, Dies|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1995/09/19/sara-shriver-community-activist-dies/dae38cf6-e061-48f1-a146-d13ed82dae6b/|date=1995-09-20|access-date=2021-01-12|issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

==Death==
Eden died on August 9, 2020,<ref name=nih/> in Tucson, Arizona,<ref name=tucson/> leaving behind a brother, Dr. Alvin Eden; 5 children and 7 grandchildren.<ref name=eecsmit/><ref name=tucson/>
